items.title: Location, Size & Extent of India
items.body:
## Position on the globe

- India lies between **8°4' N and 37°6' N** latitude and **68°7' E and 97°25' E** longitude, in South Asia.
- The **Tropic of Cancer (23½° N)** divides the country into near-equal northern (sub-tropical) and southern (tropical) halves, passing through **8 states** (Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram).
- **Indian Standard Time** is fixed on the **82°30' E** meridian (near Mirzapur), **5 h 30 min ahead of GMT**; the ~30° longitudinal spread gives a ~2-hour real time gap east to west.

## Size & dimensions

- Area **3.287 million km²** — **7th-largest** country, largest in South Asia.
- N–S extent **3,214 km**; E–W extent **2,933 km**.
- Land boundary **~15,200 km**; coastline **7,516.6 km** (Arabian Sea west, Bay of Bengal east).
- **Extremities:** northernmost **Indira Col** (Siachen), southernmost **Indira Point** (Great Nicobar). Do not confuse the two.

## Neighbours (land-border length)

| Neighbour | Border (km) |
|---|---|
| Bangladesh | 4,096 (longest) |
| China | 3,488 |
| Pakistan | 3,323 |
| Nepal | 1,751 |
| Myanmar | 1,643 |
| Bhutan | 699 |
| Afghanistan | 106 |
keyPoints: India extends 8°4'–37°6' N and 68°7'–97°25' E; Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 states.
IST is based on 82°30' E and is 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT.
India is the 7th-largest country (3.287 million km²); coastline 7,516.6 km, land border ~15,200 km.
Northernmost point = Indira Col; southernmost = Indira Point (Great Nicobar).
Longest land border is with Bangladesh (4,096 km); shortest with Afghanistan (106 km).
items.mnemonic: Border length order 'BaChiPaNeMyBhA' = Bangladesh > China > Pakistan > Nepal > Myanmar > Bhutan > Afghanistan.

figure.caption: India's land borders: Bangladesh (4,096 km) longest, Afghanistan (106 km) shortest.

items.title: The Himalayas — Ranges, Peaks & Regional Divisions
items.body:
## Longitudinal ranges (north to south)

- **Trans Himalaya** — Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar, Kailash ranges (Tibetan side); K2 (8,611 m) lies here.
- **Great Himalaya / Himadri** — loftiest, continuous, permanently snow-covered, granite core; avg ~6,000 m. Peaks: Everest (Nepal), **Kanchenjunga 8,586 m (India, highest wholly in India)**, Nanga Parbat, Nanda Devi, Namcha Barwa.
- **Lesser Himalaya / Himachal** — 3,700–4,700 m; **Pir Panjal** (longest), Dhauladhar, Mahabharat; holds Kashmir, Kullu, Kangra valleys and hill stations.
- **Shiwalik / Outer Himalaya** — 900–1,100 m; unconsolidated river sediment; **Duns** (e.g. Dehra Dun) lie between Shiwalik and Lesser Himalaya.

## Regional divisions (west to east)

- Kashmir (Karewa saffron soils, cold desert) → Himachal & Uttarakhand → Darjeeling–Sikkim (Tista; no Shiwalik) → Arunachal (Namcha Barwa, deep gorges) → **Purvanchal** (Patkai, Naga, Manipur, Mizo/Lushai hills) forming the eastern boundary.

> Himalayas are **young fold mountains**, still rising, giving antecedent rivers and deep gorges.
keyPoints: Longitudinal ranges N→S: Trans Himalaya, Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lesser), Shiwalik (Outer).
Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak lying entirely within India.
Pir Panjal is the longest range of the Lesser Himalaya; Duns lie between Shiwalik and Lesser Himalaya.
West-to-east: Kashmir → Himachal-Uttarakhand → Darjeeling-Sikkim → Arunachal → Purvanchal.
Purvanchal = Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo (Lushai) hills.
items.mnemonic: Ranges N→S 'TG-LS' = Trans, Greater (Himadri), Lesser (Himachal), Shiwalik.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Physiographic Divisions of India - Himalayas and Northern Plains

figure.alt: The four longitudinal Himalayan ranges from north to south
figure.caption: N→S ranges: Trans-Himalaya, Himadri, Himachal (Lesser), Shiwalik (Outer).

items.title: Northern Plains & the Peninsular Plateau
items.body:
## Northern Plains

- Formed by alluvium of the **Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra**; ~7 lakh km², ~2,400 km long.
- Three sections: **Punjab Plains** (Indus system), **Ganga Plains** (Ghaggar to Teesta), **Brahmaputra Plains** (Assam).
- Relief belts (N→S): **Bhabar** (narrow pebbly belt where streams vanish) → **Terai** (marshy re-emergence belt) → **Bhangar** (older alluvium, kankar nodules) → **Khadar** (younger, annually renewed floodplain, most fertile).

## Peninsular Plateau

- **Oldest and largest** division (600–900 m); irregular triangle of ancient crystalline/igneous/metamorphic rock formed from the breaking **Gondwana** landmass. **Deccan Trap** = basaltic lava (black soil).
- **Central Highlands** — north of the Narmada (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur).
- **Deccan Plateau** — south of the Narmada, tilts east; drained by Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri.
- **Vindhya** (north of Narmada) and **Satpura** (Narmada–Tapi, peak Dhupgarh 1,350 m) form the N–S divide.
- Bordered by the **Western Ghats** (continuous, higher) and **Eastern Ghats** (discontinuous, dissected by rivers).
keyPoints: Northern Plains relief belts N→S: Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar → Khadar (Khadar most fertile).
Plains formed by Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra alluvium; three sections Punjab/Ganga/Brahmaputra.
Peninsular Plateau is India's oldest and largest division, from the Gondwana landmass.
Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada; the Deccan Plateau lies south of it.
Vindhya (north of Narmada) and Satpura (Narmada–Tapi) form the north-south divide; Western Ghats are continuous, Eastern Ghats discontinuous.
items.mnemonic: Plains belts 'BT-BK' = Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar (north to south).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Physiographic Divisions of India - Himalayas and Northern Plains; Plateaus and Deserts

figure.alt: The four relief belts of the Northern Plains from north to south
figure.caption: Relief belts a river crosses: Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar → Khadar (most fertile).

items.title: Coastal Plains, Islands & the Thar Desert
items.body:
## Coastal plains (~6,000 km)

| Feature | Western Coastal Plain | Eastern Coastal Plain |
|---|---|---|
| Between | Western Ghats & Arabian Sea | Eastern Ghats & Bay of Bengal |
| Coast type | **Submergent** (natural harbours) | **Emergent** (broad, deltaic) |
| Width | Narrow (~65 km) | Wider |
| Segments | Kutch, Konkan, Karnataka (Kanara), Malabar (Kerala) | Northern Circars, Coromandel |

- The two plains meet at **Kanyakumari**. West coast has deep ports (submergence); east coast has the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery.

## Islands

- **Andaman & Nicobar** (Bay of Bengal) — **volcanic/tectonic** origin; **Barren Island** is India's only active volcano; Indira Point is the southern tip.
- **Lakshadweep** (Arabian Sea) — **coral** origin, low-lying atolls.

## Thar Desert

- The **Great Indian (Thar/Marusthali) Desert** spans Rajasthan–Gujarat; the **Great Rann of Kutch** (Gujarat) is a salt-soaked seasonal wetland; ephemeral **Luni** is the main river.
keyPoints: Western coast is submergent (good harbours); eastern coast is emergent, wider and deltaic.
West coast segments: Kutch, Konkan, Kanara, Malabar; east coast: Northern Circars, Coromandel.
Andaman & Nicobar are volcanic/tectonic (Barren Island active volcano); Lakshadweep is coral.
The two coastal plains meet at Kanyakumari.
Thar Desert lies in Rajasthan/Gujarat; the Great Rann of Kutch is a salt marsh in Gujarat.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Physiographic Divisions of India - Coastal Plains and Islands

items.title: Drainage — Himalayan vs Peninsular River Systems
items.body:
## Concepts

- **Drainage basin** = area drained by a river and tributaries; **watershed** = the dividing boundary. **Antecedent** rivers (Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra) predate Himalayan uplift and cut gorges across it.

## Himalayan rivers (perennial)

- **Indus** — rises near Mansarovar (Tibet, 'Singi Khamban'); five Punjab tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj) unite as the **Panchnad**; in India flows only through Leh (Ladakh).
- **Ganga** — 2,525 km; tributaries Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi ('Sorrow of Bihar'), Son.
- **Brahmaputra** — rises in Tibet (Tsangpo), enters via Arunachal (Dihang); braided, heavily silt-laden.

## Peninsular rivers (mostly seasonal)

- **East-flowing** into the Bay of Bengal (deltas): **Godavari** (largest peninsular river, 'Dakshin Ganga'), **Krishna**, **Kaveri**, **Mahanadi**.
- **West-flowing** into the Arabian Sea (rift-valley estuaries, no delta): **Narmada**, **Tapi**.
keyPoints: Himalayan rivers are perennial and antecedent; peninsular rivers are mostly rain-fed/seasonal.
Indus five Punjab tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj) form the Panchnad.
Godavari is the largest peninsular river ('Dakshin Ganga'); Kosi is the 'Sorrow of Bihar'.
East-flowing peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) form deltas in the Bay of Bengal.
Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea, forming estuaries not deltas.
items.mnemonic: West-flowing peninsular pair = 'NT' (Narmada, Tapi); all other majors flow East.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Drainage System - Introduction; Himalayan & Peninsular River Systems

figure.alt: Comparison of Himalayan and Peninsular river systems
figure.caption: Himalayan rivers (perennial, deltas) vs Peninsular rivers (seasonal; Narmada/Tapi flow west).

items.title: Indian Monsoon & Climate
items.body:
## The monsoon mechanism

- 'Monsoon' ← Arabic **mausim** (season); seasonal winds that reverse direction — sea→land in summer, land→sea in winter.
- **SW monsoon (June–Sept):** intense **low pressure over the Tibetan Plateau**, the **northward shift of the Subtropical Jet Stream (STJ)**, formation of the **Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)**, and the **Somali (Findlater) Jet** together trigger onset (~1st week of June over Kerala).
- Splits into the **Arabian Sea** and **Bay of Bengal** branches; a mid-season **'break'** brings dry spells.
- **NE / retreating monsoon (Oct–Dec):** high pressure builds over Tibet/Siberia and the ITCZ shifts south; winds cross the Bay of Bengal to drench the **Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu)** and coastal AP — their main rainy season.

## Interannual controls

- **El Niño** (warm central/eastern Pacific) tends to **weaken** the SW monsoon; **La Niña** strengthens it.
- A **positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)** favours a good monsoon.
keyPoints: SW monsoon onset is driven by the Tibetan low, the northward shift of the Subtropical Jet Stream and the Tropical Easterly Jet.
SW monsoon (June–Sept) has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches; onset over Kerala ~1st week of June.
The NE (retreating) monsoon brings the main rainfall to the Coromandel coast and coastal Andhra Pradesh.
El Niño generally weakens the SW monsoon; La Niña and a positive IOD strengthen it.
'Monsoon' derives from the Arabic 'mausim' meaning season.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Indian Climate I

figure.alt: Mechanism of the south-west and retreating north-east monsoons
figure.caption: SW monsoon (June–Sept) with two branches; NE/retreating monsoon (Oct–Dec) rains the Coromandel coast & coastal AP.

items.title: Soils & Natural Vegetation of India
items.body:
## Soils (ICAR: 8 groups)

| Soil | Where | Crops / notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Alluvial** | Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plain, deltas | Most extensive (~43%); potash-rich, phosphorus-poor; wheat, rice, sugarcane |
| **Black (Regur)** | Deccan Trap | Cotton; moisture-retentive, self-ploughing; rich in lime/iron, poor in N & P |
| **Red** | Low-rainfall crystalline areas | Red from ferric oxide; millets, pulses |
| **Laterite** | High heat + heavy rain uplands | Intense leaching, low humus; cashew, ragi, tea |
| **Desert** | Arid Rajasthan/Gujarat | Saline, wind-borne; bajra, barley with irrigation |

(Also forest/mountain, saline-alkaline (Usara), and marshy/bog soils.)

## Natural vegetation (by rainfall & altitude)

- **Tropical evergreen** (>200 cm): Western Ghats, NE, Andamans — rosewood, mahogany, ebony.
- **Deciduous/monsoon** (100–200 cm): most widespread — **teak**, sal.
- **Dry deciduous / thorn** (<100 / <50 cm): central India, Rajasthan — acacia, babul.
- **Tidal (mangrove):** deltas of Ganga (Sundarbans — **Sundari** tree), Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Cauvery.
- **Mountain/alpine:** conifers (pine, fir, oak) grading to alpine grasses above the tree line.
- 1988 Forest Policy target: **33%** of area under forest.
keyPoints: ICAR classifies Indian soils into 8 groups; alluvial soil is the most extensive (~43%).
Black (Regur) soil on the Deccan Trap is ideal for cotton and self-ploughs when dry.
Laterite soil forms by intense leaching under high heat and rainfall; low in humus.
Vegetation shifts with rainfall: evergreen (>200 cm) → deciduous → thorn (<50 cm); teak dominates monsoon forests.
Sundari is the key mangrove tree of the Sundarbans; the 1988 Forest Policy targets 33% forest cover.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Geography: Soils in India; Natural Vegetation of India

figure.alt: Major soil types of India and where they occur
figure.caption: Alluvial (most extensive), Black/Regur (cotton), Red, Laterite and Desert soils.

items.title: Forest Types, National Parks & Faunal Distribution
items.body:
## Forest types (Champion & Seth)

India's forests are classified into **5 major groups** and **16 type-groups**. Vegetation shifts with **rainfall** and **altitude**.

| Type | Rainfall | Trees |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical evergreen | >200 cm | rosewood, mahogany, ebony |
| Tropical moist deciduous | 100–200 cm | **sal**, teak, sandalwood |
| Tropical dry deciduous | 70–100 cm | **teak**, bamboo |
| Thorn & scrub | <70 cm | acacia (kikar), khair |
| Tidal (mangrove) | deltas/estuaries | sundari |

- **Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests** are the **most widespread** in India.
- Montane forests grade from oak/pine → deodar/silver-fir → alpine meadows with altitude.

## Wildlife conservation

- **Jim Corbett** (formerly Hailey, **1936**) = India's **first national park**.
- **Project Tiger** launched **1973** (9 reserves); run by the **NTCA**. **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam** = largest tiger reserve by area.
- **Hemis** (Ladakh) = **largest national park**; **Madhya Pradesh** = highest tiger population ('Tiger State').

## Signature faunal strongholds

| Animal | Stronghold |
|---|---|
| Asiatic Lion | Gir NP, Gujarat |
| One-horned Rhino | Kaziranga NP, Assam |
| Asiatic Wild Ass | Little Rann of Kutch |
| Hangul (Kashmir stag) | Dachigam NP, J&K |
| Great Indian Bustard | Desert NP (Rajasthan), Rollapadu (AP) |
keyPoints: Champion & Seth classify Indian forests into 5 major groups and 16 type-groups.
Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread; sal = moist deciduous, teak = dry deciduous.
Tropical evergreen forests need >200 cm rainfall; thorn/scrub grows below 70 cm.
Jim Corbett (1936) was India's first national park; Project Tiger began in 1973.
Hemis (Ladakh) is India's largest national park; MP has the highest tiger population.
Asiatic Lion = Gir; one-horned Rhino = Kaziranga; Asiatic Wild Ass = Little Rann of Kutch; Hangul = Dachigam.
items.mnemonic: Rainfall ladder for forests: Ever-Moist-Dry-Thorn = 200 / 100 / 70 / below-70 cm.
items.source: NCERT Geography — Natural Vegetation & Wildlife; NTCA; Wildlife Institute of India

figures.caption: Forest types by rainfall: evergreen (>200 cm) → moist/dry deciduous → thorn → mangrove.

items.title: High-yield Named-Fact Matches (Glaciers, Hills, Rivers, Islands, Spread)
items.body:
UPSC/APPSC love match- and multi-statement items on specific named entities. Memorise these clusters.

## Glacier → river fed

| Glacier | River | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| Gangotri (Gaumukh) | Bhagirathi (Ganga) | |
| Bandarpunch | Yamuna | |
| Bara Shigri | Chenab | |
| Milam | **Goriganga** | NOT Mandakini |
| Zemu | **Teesta** | NOT Manas |
| Siachen | Nubra | India's largest glacier |

## Peaks & hills → location

- **Namcha Barwa** → Arunachal (E Himalaya), **not Garhwal**; **Nanda Devi** → Kumaon; **Nokrek** → Meghalaya (Garo Hills), **not Sikkim**.
- **Cardamom Hills** → south Western Ghats; **Kaimur** → Vindhyan range; **Mahadeo** → Satpura; **Mikir (Karbi Anglong)** → Assam (NE).

## Rivers

- **Godavari** tributaries: **Indravati, Pranahita** (Wardha+Wainganga), Manjira, Sabari. **Pennar** and **Vamsadhara** are independent (not Godavari/Krishna tributaries).
- **Nagavali & Vamsadhara** rise in the **Eastern Ghats** (north-coastal AP/Odisha). **Teesta**'s main tributary is the **Rangeet**.
- Indus: five Punjab rivers form the **Panchnad**; the **Chenab** carries them to join the Indus.

## Islands & spread

- **Ten Degree Channel** separates **Andaman** from **Nicobar**; **Great Nicobar** is closest to **Sumatra**; **Indira Point** = southernmost point.
- **Himalayas** span **more than five** States; **Western Ghats** span **six** (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu); **Pulicat** spans **AP + Tamil Nadu**.
- **Easternmost State = Arunachal Pradesh; westernmost = Gujarat.**
- **Tea-growing States**: Assam (largest), West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, plus Himachal, Tripura and (Araku) Andhra Pradesh.
keyPoints: Glacier→river: Bandarpunch→Yamuna, Bara Shigri→Chenab, Milam→Goriganga (NOT Mandakini), Zemu→Teesta (NOT Manas), Siachen→Nubra.
Namcha Barwa is in Arunachal (not Garhwal); Nokrek is in Meghalaya (not Sikkim); Nanda Devi is in Kumaon.
Godavari tributaries include Indravati and Pranahita; Pennar and Vamsadhara are independent rivers; Nagavali & Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats.
Ten Degree Channel separates Andaman from Nicobar; Great Nicobar is closest to Sumatra; Indira Point is India's southernmost point.
Himalayas span more than five States; Western Ghats span six States; Pulicat spans AP and Tamil Nadu; easternmost State = Arunachal, westernmost = Gujarat.
Tea-growing States: Assam (largest), West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Himachal Pradesh, Tripura and Andhra Pradesh (Araku).
items.mnemonic: Milam→Goriganga, Zemu→Teesta — the two 'M/Z' traps examiners love.
items.source: UPSC CSE Prelims 2014/2015/2017/2019/2021/2022; NCERT India — Physical Environment
